Theabilitytomaintain near real-time operation of SDF algorithms has resulted in the continuous improvement of SDF systems’ capabilities as the trade-off between fidelity and complexity continuously evolves due to increases in mobile computational power, improved software design, newer algorithm types, and more data-rich sensors. In the following sections, we will briefly describe the evolution of the SDF technology (Sec. 2.1), thenmorethoroughlydocumentthemathematicalframeworkimplementedthroughSDF(Sec.2.2), and , then describe the state-of-the-art (Sec. 2.3). 2.1 Evolution of SDF Technology The concepts that formed Scene Data Fusion evolved from a series of projects at LBNL and elsewhere. Foremost, was the DHS-supported Advanced Technology Demonstrations (ATDs) called Roadside Tracker (RST) [12], Stand-off Radiation Detection System (SORDS) [13] and the Advanced Radiological Enhanced-sensor System (ARES) [14]. Road-side tracker demonstrated performance improvement in detecting R/N material in transit by correlating radiation signatures with vehicle tracks obtained by contextual sensors. One of the RST systems, Mobile Imaging and Spectroscopic Threat Identification (MISTI) [15, 16] was provided to LBNL and UC Berkeley after the RST project ended and was retrofit to become the Radiological Mobile Analysis Platform (RadMAP) [17]. RadMAP represented LBNL’s first experiments in connecting radiation imaging techniques with contextual sensors. Shortly thereafter, the ARES ATD also leveraged radiation imaging and mapping techniques in conjunction with pre-compiled terrain databases [18] and camera-based tracking [19] to demonstrate improved ability map and localize radiation sources [20]. Concurrently, LBNL undertook outfitting the high-efficiency multi-mode imager [21] with contextual sensors in order to perform contamination mapping in the evacuated area of Japan following the Fukushima Dai’ichi disaster [22]. At this point, LBNL received significant support from DTRA-NTD in order to develop SDF technology for radiological search and contamination mapping applications which resulted in the creationofthefirstLocalizationandMappingPlatform(LAMP)systems,comprisingoffourSigma- 50 detectors [23], a camera, lidar and IMU, and an Intel Nuc computer, which saved and processed online all the collected data, and served data products to a web-browser interface. Photographs of this first LAMP and its near-immediate mechanical revision are provided in Fig. 3. The system’s UI and a photo are provided in Fig. 4. The LAMP UI was initially developed to be served as a web page that can be viewed with any common web browser. This design concept has carried on to most SDF systems currently in use.
